label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
**Jonno, this one's for you (the coolroom, Cup Day)**

Jonno. Mate. You've messaged me four times asking what happened with the coolroom, so here it is in one go, and you can stop asking. Grab a cup of tea or whatever it is you drink over there now.

**6.40am, Cup Day**

Tuesday 3 November. I get in, open the coolroom door, and it feels wrong. You know that feeling, like walking into a pub toilet that's too warm. I check the thermometer and it says 11 degrees.

Eleven. For anyone who isn't a chef, that's not a coolroom, that's a nice spring day in Melbourne. The compressor had carked it sometime overnight and nobody knew.

We had 140 booked for Cup Day lunch. Set menu, three courses. Raff was away, so it was me running the show.

**The plan, such as it was**

I rang Wally from Coldline. Lovely bloke, very calm, the calmness of a man who is not in your kitchen. He couldn't get out until Wednesday, and the part was coming from Sydney. So that was a full service on no coolroom, with the part presumably arriving by pigeon.

Then I told Phil. Phil listened carefully and said, "Just make it work mate."

That is not a plan, Phil. A plan has steps. That's a vibe.

Anyway, here's what "make it work" looked like:

- Everything that could live in the two undercounters went in the two undercounters
- Everything that couldn't went in the bar fridge
- Everything else went next door, because Marta from the cafe took one look at my face and gave us half her walk-in

Marta is a saint and I will be paying for it for the rest of my life, but more on that in a bit.

**The beef shin incident**

You would've loved this. We had 30kg of beef shin that needed to get to Marta's, and the only way to move it was down the laneway. Me and Benny found a milk crate on a trolley, loaded it up, and set off. In the rain, obviously, because God has a sense of humour.

Halfway down the laneway one of the wheels fell off.

So picture it. Two grown men in checked pants and aprons, rain coming down, trying to keep 30kg of beef shin balanced on a three-wheeled milk crate while a wheel rolls off toward the bins. Benny was swearing in a way I can't repeat on a blog my mum reads. We got there. The shin was fine. Our dignity was not.

And then, because the universe wasn't done, a lady on table 9 spotted us through the window and asked the floor staff whether the beef was "free range from the laneway."

Yes, madam. Laneway-raised. Grass fed, if you count the weeds.

**Kev and the ice**

Dishy Kev, who I want on record as the hero of this story, took the old esky down to the servo and came back with 14 bags of ice. Fourteen. The servo guy asked him if we were having a party.

Kev said "something like that."

We filled the esky and it became a fridge. This is what bistro kitchens actually run on, mate: bar fridges and spite. You'd know this if you hadn't gone soft.

**The panna cotta**

At 12.15 I had to 86 the panna cotta. It's dairy, it had been sitting in the warm, and I wasn't about to poison anyone on the one day of the year everyone's already a bit loose.

So dessert became "affogato with whatever." Whatever we had. Ice cream, coffee, a biscuit, a bit of something. And I swear to you, people loved it more than the panna cotta. Table after table. One bloke asked if it was a new menu item. I said yes. It is now.

I'm not saying the panna cotta was bad. I'm saying I've spent weeks perfecting it and a shot of coffee over ice cream beat it in about four minutes. I'm choosing to laugh about it.

**The damage**

About $1800 in stock gone, mostly dairy and the duck legs. The duck legs hurt. I'm not over the duck legs. Phil, to his credit, didn't say a word about it, which from Phil is basically a hug.

Marta got paid back in croissant credit, which means I now owe her roughly three weeks of staff meal. She's got a spreadsheet. I've seen it.

Oh, and I had a horse in the sweep. Ice Cold Lad. I swear I'm not making this up. He came second last. The universe wasn't just taking the piss that day, it was doing a full stand-up set.

**The thing is, though**

It was the best service we did all year.

I don't know how else to say it. Everyone was locked in. Nobody was standing around. Nobody was grumbling. When the whole kitchen knows it's going to be a disaster, something clicks, and every single person just goes. Benny was flying. Kev was a machine. The floor were calm. We sent out 140 covers off a bar fridge, an esky and half a cafe walk-in, and I don't think a single table knew anything was wrong, apart from the laneway lady.

Wally turned up Wednesday, the part had arrived, and the coolroom is back to a lovely 3 degrees. I've been checking it every morning like it's a newborn.

**So, Jonno**

You would've lost your mind. Honestly. You'd have been on grill with the beef shin all over you, the esky leaking, and you'd have gone full meltdown by about 10am. You'd have cried. You've gone soft over there, I can tell from the way you've been messaging. Back when you were here you'd have just laughed and kept cooking.

Anyway. That's the story. No more messages about it. If you want to hear it again, you can come back and I'll tell you in person, with a beer, at a pub that doesn't charge you nine quid a pint.

Come home, ya flog.
